questions.prompt: What is the perfect pitch in this chapter?
choices: A long presentation with every principle named out loud
An integrated sequence where each move prepares the next
A script that never changes across rooms

explanation.gentle: The perfect pitch is one sequence, not many separate tricks.
explanation.direct: Correct. Klaff treats the perfect pitch as an integrated STRONG flow.
explanation.competitive: The win is sequence, not a pile of tactics.

questions.prompt: Why does brevity matter so much here?
choices: Because shorter always sounds smarter
Because it keeps one stage from stealing energy from the next
Because audiences dislike stories

explanation.gentle: Brevity protects the handoff from one move to the next.
explanation.direct: The chapter links brevity to rhythm and energy transfer.
explanation.competitive: Shorter matters because flow dies when one stage overruns the rest.

questions.prompt: What usually happens when one stage of the pitch grows too large?
choices: The whole sequence can lose rhythm
The audience automatically trusts the presenter more
The method becomes easier to follow

explanation.gentle: An oversized stage can crowd out the later moves.
explanation.direct: The sequence breaks when one part takes too much space.
explanation.competitive: If one beat hogs the room, the flow collapses.

questions.prompt: A founder keeps adding proof after the hookpoint. What is the likely result?
choices: The peak and close both get stronger
The peak can lose force and crowd the close
The frame becomes more stable

explanation.gentle: Too much proof after the peak can weaken the later handoff.
explanation.direct: The chapter warns that extra explanation after hookpoint steals force from the close.
explanation.competitive: Stuffing proof after the summit can flatten the finish.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with turning integration into recap?
choices: It makes the audience experience the method more directly
It turns the pitch into commentary about the method instead of the method working
It automatically shortens the pitch too much

explanation.gentle: Recap talks about the method instead of letting the method work.
explanation.direct: The room should feel the sequence, not hear a lecture about it.
explanation.competitive: If you explain the machine instead of running it, the pitch loses force.

questions.prompt: In a school defense, why can repeated setup be harmful?
choices: It gives every later stage more energy
It can stall the room and drain momentum from the rest of the sequence
It removes the need for a close

explanation.gentle: Repeated setup can keep the audience from moving forward.
explanation.direct: Restarting the explanation weakens the live rhythm.
explanation.competitive: Every rewind taxes the runway the rest of the pitch needs.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter say about script worship?
choices: One perfect script should work in every room
A strong presenter needs no structure at all
Structure matters, but the sequence must stay responsive to the room

explanation.gentle: The method gives structure, but it should not become a rigid script.
explanation.direct: The chapter rejects both chaos and robotic repetition.
explanation.competitive: Use the structure, but do not let it freeze you.

questions.prompt: What is a better sign of mastery than polished wording alone?
choices: Being able to keep the sequence moving under pressure
Using more slides than competitors
Memorizing the longest version of the pitch

explanation.gentle: Mastery shows up when the flow stays intact.
explanation.direct: Sequence control under pressure matters more than polished lines by themselves.
explanation.competitive: Pretty lines mean less than momentum that survives contact.

questions.prompt: What is the deepest limit on the idea of a perfect pitch?
choices: It should be a rigid script that never changes
It cannot ignore the room or become mechanical
It should always maximize complexity

explanation.gentle: The sequence should stay alive and responsive, not robotic.
explanation.direct: The chapter says perfect means controlled, not mechanical.
explanation.competitive: A dead script is not mastery. Responsive structure is.

questions.prompt: Why does this chapter lead naturally into the final chapter?
choices: Because repeatable control matters more than one polished performance
Because the next chapter abandons the method entirely
Because the book returns to chapter summaries only

explanation.gentle: The next chapter turns sequence control into a lasting capability shift.
explanation.direct: Integration points toward mastery that can be repeated, not just one good pitch.
explanation.competitive: The real win is becoming the person who can run the room on purpose.
